item.title: Why We Care So Much About People We Have Never Met
item.description:
Parasocial Relationships

Why We Care So Much About People We Have Never Met

The psychology behind our fascination with celebrities’ weddings, babies, and breakups.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Parasocial relationships can make celebrities feel psychologically familiar to us.
  • Repeated exposure on social media can strengthen the sense that we genuinely “know” a celebrity.
  • That feeling of intimacy has commercial value and is being exploited by marketers.

Lately, I have been working on an ongoing research project on influencer marketing, which means that I have spent an unreasonable amount of time reading research on why people follow, trust, and buy things from people they have never met. While working through the literature on parasocial relationships, I found myself thinking about the phenomenon somewhat less academically—namely, why I so desperately wanted to marry Robbie Williams when I was a teenager.

This was not a particularly reciprocal relationship, as Robbie Williams did not know that I existed, which presented some obvious logistical problems for our future together. I, on the other hand, knew quite a lot about him. And although my teenage obsession eventually disappeared, the phenomenon certainly did not. We still want to know all the details of Taylor Swift’s marriage, what the latest royal baby looks like, who has broken up with whom, and whether two people we have never met are secretly feuding.

Why do we care? Psychologists and media researchers have been asking versions of this question for decades. And the answer has a lot to do with the curious ability of our minds to turn repeated encounters with strangers into something that feels like a relationship.

The Friends Who Don't Know Us

The idea dates back to the work of Donald Horton and Richard Wohl in the 1950s. Parasocial relationships describe the one-sided, friendship-like bonds we can develop with media personalities through repeated exposure. The more we see someone and learn about their lives, the more familiar they become. And eventually we can start to feel that we actually know them.

Communication scholars Siyoung Chung and Hichang Cho describe understanding as the feeling that we know a celebrity personally and understand their values and motivations. Repeated exposure, particularly when celebrities communicate in a direct and intimate way, can create a sense of closeness that makes us begin to think of them almost as friends.

Social Media Changed the Game

While my teenage parasocial romance required some effort (there were only magazines to buy and television appearances to catch), today's celebrities live in our pockets. Social media has dramatically narrowed the psychological distance between celebrities and their audiences. Instead of occasionally seeing a carefully staged interview, now we don’t even need to leave the comfort of our bed to watch our favorite celebrity make breakfast, complain about jet lag, celebrate a birthday, introduce a boyfriend, announce a pregnancy, show us their dog, and tell us how they are feeling.

Why are they oversharing so much, you might wonder? Because what looks like oversharing can also be good strategy, as research shows that self-disclosure is one of the ways we build relationships. For example, researchers Jihyun Kim and Hayeon Song studied 429 people who followed celebrities on Twitter and found that when celebrities shared details about both their work and their personal lives, followers felt closer to them, as if the celebrity were actually there with them. That sense of closeness, in turn, strengthened the feeling of having a relationship with the celebrity.

While in ordinary relationships self-disclosure (the gradual revelation of our feelings, beliefs, experiences, and private lives) is one of the processes through which intimacy develops, social media allows celebrities to reproduce some of those same cues at enormous scale. A photograph from a family holiday or a post about heartbreak may be instantly broadcast to 50 million people, but we encounter it individually, on the same little screen where our actual friends tell us about their lives.

When Familiarity Breeds Contempt

However, it is not all rainbows and unicorns. Greater exposure also gives us more opportunities to encounter things we dislike. Research shows that greater interaction on social media can sometimes make a celebrity seem less trustworthy. In other words, familiarity can breed contempt, and parasocial relationships are a double-edged sword. Marketing scholar Rebecca Mardon and colleagues found that former fans of social-media influencers sometimes become highly engaged anti-fans when the intimacy they once felt begins to erode or feel commercially exploitative. Rather than simply unfollowing, some continue to follow and discuss the influencers only now to criticize them.

You see, feeling that we know someone does not necessarily mean liking them. Parasocial relationships can keep us invested both in celebrities we adore and those we cannot stand.

Your Attention Is The Currency That Keeps the Industry Going

Parasocial relationships have economic value, and marketers are very interested in understanding how these relationships can be cultivated. Marketing professor Lauren Labrecque’s research on consumer-brand relationships in online environments notably shows that communication that feels personal, open, and responsive can make an online interaction feel more like a social relationship, and that this perceived connection can translate into greater loyalty and willingness to engage.

You see, to us as consumers scrolling through social media over our morning coffee, these glimpses into someone’s relationships, family, or breakfast can accumulate into a genuine feeling of intimacy. From a marketing perspective, however, that same intimacy is valuable because feeling connected can influence what we pay attention to and whom we trust, and ultimately how we behave. In other words, this connection can be monetized by companies that want to sell you more and more stuff you may not necessarily need.

None of this means we should stop caring about celebrities, and it makes perfect sense that the more we see of someone’s life, the more familiar they start to feel. What has changed, however, is how much of their lives we now get to see, and how deliberately that sense of closeness can be cultivated.

By all means, follow the weddings, babies, breakups, and feuds. I certainly have no grounds to judge, as I have occasionally stopped for a cup of tea and a social-media scroll in the middle of writing this post. Although, like a typical Millennial these days, my feed seems to contain more bullet journaling, medieval Byzantine poetry of Early Church Fathers, and healthy lifestyles than celebrities’ personal lives.

But remember that there is an entire marketing industry devoted to understanding how that feeling of closeness works and how to strengthen it, making your attention a central part of the business model.

item.title: A Dog Is Never "Just a Dog": How to Form Deep and Kind Bonds
item.description:
Animal Behavior

A Dog Is Never "Just a Dog": How to Form Deep and Kind Bonds

In "More Than Just a Dog," Simon Wooler stresses compassion and respect.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Dog behavior is their language; misinterpreting it leads to mutual misunderstanding.
  • Sometimes dogs don't understand what we want them to do because we don't understand them.
  • Taking the dog's point of view is essential to forming deep, respectful, and reciprocal bonds.
Source: Michal Petráš/Pexels

I recently learned of a highly-acclaimed book by force-free dog trainer Simon Wooler titled More Than Just a Dog: Understanding, loving and living with dogs: An essential guide for humans. Among Wooler's goals is for people to form deep, respectful, and reciprocal bonds with dogs by demystifying the science behind dog behavior—a goal I fully share—and to educate them and explain how they learn, how they tell us what they want and need from us, and the factors that influence the sort of relationship they form with us. Here's some sage advice for making meaningful connections with our canine companions and for them to return the favor.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write More Than Just a Dog and how did you come up with the title?

Simon Wooler: I was approached by the publishers, HarperCollins, when I was working with Sophie from Romania, the profoundly fearful Romanian rescue who had been adopted by author and broadcaster Rory Cellan-Jones and his wife Diane Coyle. Rory had posted about Sophie on social media and her story went viral. I was posting alongside, explaining the approach to helping Sophie and giving context to her behaviour and the progress we were making. The title started off as just a working title, but then it seemed right. It summed up the importance of the relationship many, if not most of us, have with our dogs. But as important for me was the subtitle. I didn’t want to write a ‘how to train’ book. I wanted to help people understand more about how dogs relate to their environment, how they communicate, and most importantly, how they learn, because that’s at the heart of living in harmony with our dogs.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

SW: My interest in dog behaviour started with Thomson, a fearful and aggressive Rottweiler who I inexplicably made a connection with at a local shelter and decided to adopt. It became quickly clear that the conventional training techniques were not going to help us. That’s when I found Jean Donaldson’s Academy for Dog Trainers. My life changed from working in a world where everything operated at pace and success is obvious and audible to a world where I have to take everything patiently, step-by-step, where the dog sets the pace and I have to be tuned in to every micro-step of improvement so that I can build on it.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

SW: People who love dogs and want to know more, both those living in happy harmony and those wrestling with behavioural challenges. For any dog lover, I hope it offers some ‘aha’ moments of enlightenment, if that’s not too pompous a word.

Source: HarperElement, used with permission

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

SW: Overall, the book looks at how dogs learn (and how we can use that knowledge to build training into the everyday), the influence of nature vs nurture on dog behaviour, interpreting body language, and navigating major life changes as well as understanding and responding to specific behavioural issues like fear, reactivity, and aggression.

In terms of big messages, the first is that for dogs, behaviour is language, pretty much the only one they have to communicate what they need. Putting very human spins on the way they behave—spite, defiance, dominance—can leave us locked in mutual incomprehension. Working on our fluency in interpreting dog behaviour is essential. After all, living harmoniously with another species is no small thing.

Others are: Dogs do what works for them. Their motivations are no more sinister than that. If a behaviour is rewarding, they’ll do more of it. If we consistently offer reward for the behaviours we want, they’re happy to work for pay. We don’t need physical punishment, shouting, scaring, or shocks. Our relationship with our dogs shouldn’t be an endless battle of wills.

Agency is important. We put boundaries around our dogs’ lives as soon as they set paw over the threshold. Mainly, they’re necessary to keep them safe and for the smooth functioning of household and community. But we should allow them some agency. For fearful dogs, agency is crucial. It builds curiosity, learning capacity, and emotional regulation. But being able to exercise some agency is good for all dogs, too. Giving them choices about who they interact with and how, for example—not forcing encounters with other dogs or people when they’re reluctant.

Fear is not a choice. Fear is an emotion. It may not seem rational to us, but it’s very real. It’s not ‘bad behaviour’ and we can’t simply make them ‘get over it’ by confronting whatever causes anxiety. We have to go slowly, at their pace, building positive associations and establishing the home and family unit as a secure base from which they can gradually grow confidence to explore more of the world.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

SW: I wanted to make the rich but complex field of behaviour accessible to people who aren’t science geeks, add a touch of humour and storytelling, drawing on the dogs and people I’ve worked with.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about how to teach their dogs to live in harmony with them, they will work hard to establish give-and-take relationships with them and factor in what the dogs want to do and getting their consent whenever possible?

SW: Yes. It’s wonderful that most people now regard their dogs as part of the family, but that has brought with it whole new set of expectations of their behaviour, too. We want to be able to go anywhere with them—cafés, hotels, cinemas. They’ve been remarkably adaptive. But if we understand how their behaviour is shaped, I hope we cut them some slack. Give them some agency as I described before. They are our loved companions with all their quirks. Let’s not expect them, as Mary Poppins would have it, to be practically perfect in every way.

item.title: Why You Shouldn't Try to "Get Over" Grief
item.description:
Grief

Why You Shouldn't Try to "Get Over" Grief

Personal Perspective: We need to process and integrate grief into our lives, not get over it.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • If you're grieving, you may get advice telling you to "get over it" or "move on."
  • But this is both unhelpful and unrealistic. Grief is a process which takes as long as it needs.
  • If you let grief flow, and integrate the loss into your life, the pain can transform into bearable sadness.

Living a human life means we will all feel grief, at some point. This may start when we're very young, perhaps with the loss of a beloved pet or grandparent, but if we are lucky enough to move through life's seasons as intended, these losses will begin to mount up as we age.

In fact, the Buddha taught over 2,500 years ago that to be human is to suffer—this is an inevitable aspect of our existence. We grow older, get sick, lose people we love and our lives will eventually end.

Source: Diego PH/Unsplash

But the Buddha also taught that we often turn this inevitable suffering into an optional but far greater suffering through our response to it. Trying to "get over" grief is likely to do just that.

The Therapist Who Saved My Life

The heart of my new book, Heal Your Trauma: How to Overcome a Painful Childhood to Become Happy and Whole Again, is the story of how I have spent the last 30-plus years healing from the sudden, traumatic loss of my father when I was just 24. I had been living in Asia for two years and he died before I could get home. This was, by far, the worst thing that has ever happened to me—the grief was overwhelming. And as a young man, I didn't have the tools to deal with it. I had barely cried since I was a child (men didn't cry, in my day) and so couldn't process this heavy, hard rock of pain in my chest.

After months of carrying this rock around, I eventually sought counselling from a family friend, Huli. And this wise, kind man helped me begin to dissolve that rock, first in our sessions and then my daily life. I allowed myself to grieve, finally—and to cry. I can honestly say this wonderful man helped save my life, because I just couldn't go on like that; it was too hard.

And the silver lining of that very dark cloud was that he suggested I train as a counsellor, which I had never considered until that day but given the beautiful nature of our work, I was intrigued. That led me to my first therapy training, in psychosynthesis, a transpersonal model that valued the spiritual component of the human heart and mind. It was also a powerful, experiential training so I spent three years in that wonderful group of people, processing and moving through my grief.

At the time, especially after a few months, well-meaning people started advising me to "move on" with my life, or "get over it," as if that were remotely possible. We still see variations of this advice in the media, both social and mainstream, as if there is some kind of time limit on grief: OK, it's been a year now, time to stop crying and get over it. This is both unrealistic and unhelpful, because we need to grieve—in our own, unique way—for as long as it takes. The grieving process can't be forced, or rushed.

Grief Is a Natural, Healthy Process

In fact, your mind and body knows exactly how to grieve. That's because grief is an inherent part of life, not somehow separate from it. We see it throughout he animal kingdom, because humans are not unique in grieving those we love—elephants, chimps, horses, dogs, and whales are among the creatures thought to feel and show grief. We know how to grieve like we know how to love, to eat, to breathe.

The problem often comes when we experience "complex grief," like I felt with my dad, because we had a complicated relationship. I felt as much anger and frustration with him as I did sadness at his loss, which made it even harder to let those tears flow. Problems can also arise when grief is traumatic, like that triggered by losing someone far too young—the loss of a child, for example, is one of the hardest things any person has to bear, and can completely derail your life.

In these circumstances, the grief can get stuck—like that heavy rock in my chest—and you may need the help of a kind, skilled professional to get unstuck, as I did. And with a little help you can clear the internal obstacles out of the way and let that grief flow through you, in whatever way it needs to: crying, raging, hating God for being so cruel, hating the person you lost for leaving you, letting the torrent of pain and hurt move through you.

And if you can do that, as I have learned over these three decades, it's not that you ever get over grief but it does become lighter, more bearable. When I think of my dad, I always feel sad and regretful that I lost him so young, that he never got to meet my wonderful son, who he would have adored. But that's OK, because I should feel sad. Losing a parent is a profoundly sad thing to happen, whatever stage of life you might be in.

But that raw, heavy, unbearable pain is gone. I let it flow through me and it naturally faded with time. That's how it should be.

If you have recently lost someone and are still in that agonising early stage, I'm so sorry. I know only too well how hard that is to bear. But hold on. Trust that it will get easier, with time. And if it feels stuck, or too much to bear, please do get some help from a kind, compassionate person—take it from me, it could be life-changing.

item.title: The Irony of Conspirituality: Politics and Purity
item.description:
Spirituality

The Irony of Conspirituality: Politics and Purity

Musical manifestations: How a band's name became a psychological term.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • New research reveals the link between conspiracy theories and spirituality.
  • Conspirituality began as a Canadian hip-hop group's name and later was used academically.
  • The findings surrounding purity have also been seen in religious communities.

My work as a belief psychologist and parapsychologist often puts me in situations where I encounter people who hold unusual and sometimes dangerous beliefs. I started noticing something in the town where I live: People who identified as spiritual seemed unusually susceptible to conspiracy beliefs.

This got me thinking about the New Age wellness movement, which, according to the Global Wellness Institute, is now a $6.8 trillion global industry that includes brands like Gwyneth Paltrow's GOOP. It's also visible in individual figures like Russell Brand, whose own political and religious views have shifted markedly rightward in recent years. I wanted to look at this connection between spirituality and conspiracy belief a bit further, and after some research, I realised somebody had beaten me to the punch and already come up with a term: conspirituality.

Canadian Hip Hop

Charlotte Ward and David Voas looked at spirituality and its relationship with conspiracy beliefs in their 2011 study titled The Emergence of Conspirituality. They used the term "conspirituality" in an academic sense. Ward and Voas saw conspirituality as a reflection of spiritual people's dissatisfaction with the political system, which kind of backed up my thoughts on the subject.

I also wanted to include another aspect: the idea of moral purity, in this context, a gut sense that something is unnatural or contaminated. But when I did the study, I hadn't realised that Ward framed conspirituality as part of a hopeful spiritual awakening, rather than something that needed scrutinising. The term itself is actually credited to a Canadian hip hop group, Conspirituality, back in 2004, fused conspiracy theory with spiritual and esoteric themes as part of the music, rather than Ward and Voas's later psychological concept.

The Paper Behind the Paper

While researching further for this post, I found there was some controversy surrounding the original 2011 paper. According to Hannah Dick (2026), the paper was mainly written by Ward, and Voas, an eminent sociologist in the area, was brought on to give it academic clout. It turned out that Ward might actually be involved in conspiritualist-type behaviours herself. Ward and Voas refer to believers as "clients" in their paper, and don't scrutinise the antisemitic tropes underpinning some of the conspiracy theories they cite, including Icke's "lizard people" theory.

Dick's article, published that April, flagged this problem. Beres, Remski, and Walker had actually got there first, uncovering Ward's insider status on their Conspirituality podcast back in 2022, and again in their 2023 book. I hadn't picked up on any of it, and with hindsight, I really should have. But just because the term conspirituality has been contested doesn't mean it's any less valid. In fact, it probably makes it all the more interesting.

It's Not Just Spirituality Causing the Problem

To explore this more, I did a study with my colleagues Chris Howard and Stu Rimmer, published in the Journal of Scientific Exploration. We used a number of scales to ask 240 people how spiritual they were, how strongly they believed in COVID-19 and other conspiracy theories, how much they valued purity, and where they sat politically. Spirituality, purity, and right-wing political views together were strong predictors of COVID-19 conspiracy belief. But we also tested whether purity and political orientation explained that relationship. The answer was partly yes: Political orientation explained it for COVID-specific beliefs, but not for general conspiracy belief. Purity, though, explained it in both: the one factor that mattered no matter which conspiracy belief we were looking at.

How It Connects

The variables could also be working serially, rather than in parallel: spirituality seems to nudge people toward valuing purity, which pushes their politics further right, which in turn predicts conspiracy belief. As far as I know, this is the first study to test that mechanism empirically, though it's worth remembering our design was correlational, so we can't say for certain it's actually causal; that would need experimental work to confirm.

Why This Matters

These findings have implications for public health messaging, for example, around cholesterol-lowering statins. Recently, false information has been making the rounds, claiming that statins cause dementia. A recent meta-analysis (Westphal Filho et al., 2025, pooling 55 studies and 7 million patients) showed that statins reduce dementia risk rather than causing it. So where does this belief come from? Not the evidence, clearly.

Part of it is that gut sense of purity itself isn't purely innate; wellness marketing spends a lot of energy selling the idea that certain foods, medicines, or interventions are "unnatural" or "contaminated," priming exactly that response. Same story with the mRNA-vaccine-causes-autism claim, which a February 2026 study also found no evidence for.

It's not just an issue in wellness circles either; Dick's study looked at a very different, more religious group (the Church of God Restoration) and found that believers in this group who are driven by purity beliefs refuse the vaccine, too, matching our study.

Isn't It Ironic, Don't You Think?

It would appear that Ward wasn't studying conspirituality from the outside; she was living it. A term that came from a Canadian hip hop group is now being used to examine the world she was part of, whether that's investigative podcasters using it to dismantle wellness grifters or empirical studies like mine looking at it from a psychologist's point of view.

But it was Beres, Remski, and Walker's podcast, the very people who use the term "conspirituality" regularly, who did the digging that uncovered Ward's insider status in the first place. Another level of irony? Thanks to Alanis Morissette, I never know what irony is anymore.

I went into this study without realising how tangled the term's own history was, and in hindsight, I probably should have caught it. But that doesn't change what the data actually showed: It's purity and politics, not spirituality alone, driving conspiracy belief.

item.title: Who Taught You to Want What You Want?
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Who Taught You to Want What You Want?

Deleuze, desire, and the psychology of capitalism.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Capitalism shapes desire—not only what we buy but also what we value, pursue, and become.
  • If we rethink desire as productive, we can explore what our desires create, reproduce, and make possible.
  • To affirm life is not simply to accept the world as it is. It is to ask what else might become possible.

The French philosopher Gilles Deleuze (1925–1995) was one of the 20th century's most influential philosophers. His philosophy can be described as a nonjudgmental, affirmative approach that aims to become worthy of what happens.

In Difference and Repetition, Deleuze sees the task of philosophy as “a liberation of thought from those images which imprison it.”

One thing that can imprison and control thought and life is capitalism.

Together with the psychiatrist Félix Guattari, Deleuze published Anti-Oedipus (2000) and A Thousand Plateaus (1987)—both books share the same subtitle: Capitalism and Schizophrenia. In this sense, the title already points toward the problem and the solution: How do social and economic systems organize our desires, and how might desire escape those forms of organization? This is also where psychoanalysis enters the picture.

What Desire Does

Anti-Oedipus is, among other things, a radical critique of psychoanalysis and particularly of what Deleuze and Guattari regarded as the reduction of desire to the Oedipal triangle of father, mother, and child. Rather than asking only what desire means, they ask what desire does. What does it produce? What does it connect? What kinds of lives does it make possible?

For Deleuze and Guattari, desire is productive. It is not simply a response to something we lack. Desire connects bodies, objects, ideas, institutions, technologies, money, and social relations. The unconscious is therefore not merely a private theatre hidden inside the individual. Desire is social and political. It is constantly connecting us to the world around us. This has important consequences for how we think about capitalism.

Capitalism's Influence

Capitalism does not only organize our labor. It also enters our desires. It teaches us what to want, what to value, what to admire, and, increasingly, what kind of person we should become. The question is therefore not only: What do I desire? It is also: Who or what has taught me to desire what I desire?

Deleuze and Guattari described capitalism as a flow of labor and capital, means of payment and financing currency, scientific and technological codes, and the market. In short: labor, money, and status. The problem with capitalism can be viewed through Deleuze’s two fundamental ontological concepts: difference and repetition. Deleuze claims that the flow of life is difference itself. “Life is the process of difference,” as Deleuze writes in Bergsonism. Yet capitalism repeats the same.

In other words: The capitalist market controls. An example could be TripAdvisor, an online travel company that organizes consumers’ experiences, making it easier for new consumers to decide—that is, to do the same, or, in business language, confirm best practice. Deleuze would most likely say: “People tend to confuse winning freedom with conversion to capitalism.”

When We Think of Ourselves as Projects

The same mechanism often appears in our understanding of ourselves. We are increasingly encouraged to think of ourselves as projects: to improve our skills, our bodies, our productivity, our careers, our relationships, and even our psychological well-being. We monitor ourselves, evaluate ourselves, and compare ourselves with others. The question becomes: Am I enough? And because there is always another achievement, another status position, another experience, another purchase, or another version of ourselves to become, we can always postpone the answer. Here capitalism and psychology meet.

The individual may experience the problem as a personal one: I am stressed. I am not successful enough. I lack confidence. I need to become more resilient. I need to optimize myself. But Deleuze and Guattari invite us to ask another question: What if some of what I experience as my personal desire has already been organized by the social world in which I live? This does not mean that psychological suffering is “caused by capitalism” in any simple sense. Depression, anxiety, burnout and other forms of suffering have complex causes, including biological, psychological, relational and social factors. But it does mean that psychology cannot always afford to look only inside the individual.

When a person repeatedly asks, “What is wrong with me?” another question may be necessary: What kind of world am I being asked to adapt to?

Deleuze and Guattari tried to overcome forms of codification by resisting the tendency to subject themselves to external—often capitalist and normative—forces, and by connecting themselves with more unconventional forms of life. Their concern was therefore not simply to reject society. It was to create different connections and different possibilities for living. The problem with capitalism is not only that it can produce greed and inequalities. It can also shape the psychological conditions under which we live. When our value becomes tied to productivity, recognition, status, and economic worth, the self can become trapped in a never-ending process of evaluation. This is where the idea of desire becomes important again.

If Desire Is Productive

If desire is understood primarily as lack, then there will always be something missing. We need another achievement, another possession, another recognition, another improvement. But if desire is productive, as Deleuze and Guattari suggest, then the question changes. Instead of asking only how we can satisfy our desires, we can ask what our desires are producing.

  • What kind of person am I becoming through what I desire?
  • What kind of relationships do my desires produce?
  • What kind of society do they reproduce?
  • What other forms of life might they make possible?

This is also why Deleuze and Guattari’s use of the term “schizophrenia” needs to be handled carefully. Clinical schizophrenia is a serious psychiatric condition and should not be confused with the philosophical concept developed in Anti-Oedipus. Their “schizophrenic” is not simply a description of a person with schizophrenia. It functions as a philosophical figure for desire escaping established forms of organization and producing new connections. According to Deleuze and Guattari, capitalism has made reality unreal by constantly reorganizing the flows of money, labor, technology, and desire. These flows affect how a person thinks, feels, and behaves, just as they affect how a society educates, governs, and organizes itself. For the same reason, Deleuze (1995) described contemporary society—already in the 1990s—as one governed by control.

People can become trapped by monetary categories such as “human capital” and “human resources,” or by playing the never-ending status game that produces what Alain de Botton has called “status anxiety”: the fear of not being worth enough, not having enough recognition, or not having sufficient market value.

The danger is that economic value becomes confused with human value. If I am only worth what I can produce, then what happens when I can no longer produce? If my identity depends upon recognition, what happens when recognition disappears? If my life is organized around becoming more valuable, when am I allowed simply to live? This is perhaps one of the psychological questions hidden within Deleuze’s philosophy. The problem is not that we have desires. Nor is the solution to eliminate desire. The question is whether our desires have become captured by a system that continually tells us that we are not yet enough.

Deleuze’s philosophy is, among many other things, an attempt to move beyond capitalism’s logic of credit and debit, value and measurement, repetition and control, by setting free what has been kept imprisoned.

To affirm life is therefore not simply to accept the world as it is. It is to ask what else might become possible.

item.title: The Real Reason Organisational Change Doesn’t Stick
item.description:
Leadership

The Real Reason Organisational Change Doesn’t Stick

How leaders can turn knowledge into lasting change.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Knowing what to do isn’t enough. New ideas need to be applied consistently and given time to produce evidence.
  • People often abandon change while it still feels uncomfortable and before the results become visible.
  • Change is sustainable when new behaviours become part of how people see themselves and how we work together.

Why do some businesses thrive while others struggle?

The strategy may be sound.

The people can be bright.

The effort is real.

Yet, somehow, things don’t seem to move forward.

In last month’s post, we explored why learning often fails to lead to behavioural change. The problem is that insight alone rarely changes behaviour.

The same problem exists at an organisational level. Even after insight has landed, there is still work to do. Why do capable people and organisations still struggle to convert understanding into performance?

Knowing What to Do Isn’t the Same as Doing It

As we demonstrated last month, the problem isn’t necessarily knowing what to do; it’s understanding how to apply it. Access to information, particularly in business, is already broad given the number of business books and articles published every year. AI has accelerated that dramatically.

Most of us can access strategies, ideas, frameworks, and user studies instantly.

Knowledge no longer provides us with the edge it once did. The advantage increasingly lies with those who apply what they learn consistently, and for long enough to make a difference.

Rob Nicklin, co-author of The Growth Code, explained,

“Understanding something is not the same as becoming it. You’ve got the information, but that’s not the same as the behaviour required to actually make that information stick. Action is effort, outcomes are evidence.

“Too many people are just doing stuff, and they give up before the evidence has started to reveal itself. You’ve got to stay in the system long enough. You keep doing the work, you build up that latent potential and, eventually, the evidence shows.”

In The Growth Code, Nicklin and his co-author, Lesley Everett, introduce The Evidence Curve to describe the gap between putting in effort and seeing enough observable evidence to reinforce the behaviour. The curve illustrates the challenge of people abandoning new approaches when effort is visible, but results are not.

The Evidence Curve™
Source: (©) The Growth Code™ Used with permission

This isn’t simply about persistence. It’s about being OK with the discomfort of continuing a behaviour before enough evidence reassures us it works. Last month, we explored how we start to resist new ideas when they conflict with our established identity. Even after we decide to try something new, a vulnerable period follows when the old behaviour still feels more natural, and the new one hasn't produced enough evidence to justify itself.

This is when many people give up, revert to comfortable ways of operating, and stifle their potential.

Reading the Room and Adapting Accordingly

Once we begin applying, not just absorbing, information, another issue emerges. We can’t just apply our new ideas blindly; we need to read the room.

Smart people armed with the best knowledge can still struggle to apply their ideas in the right way. Complex scenarios often demand different responses, but people can easily rely on familiar strengths. For example, a highly analytical person may keep looking for more data when a situation requires more empathy.

Or we may just look to what worked before and seek to replicate it. Expertise can become a weakness if it simply encourages us to repeat yesterday’s successful response in today’s different context.

Another model Nicklin and Everett introduce is The Intelligence Seesaw.

The Intelligence Seesaw™
Source: (©) The Growth Code™ Used with permission

The model illustrates the different types of intelligence everyone can bring to a situation, including:

  • IQ: intellectual/analytical intelligence
  • EQ: emotional intelligence
  • SQ: social intelligence
  • CQ: cultural intelligence
  • AQ: adaptability

Nicklin explained the importance of CQ and AQ in this model, noting that cultural intelligence helps us read the room and adaptability enables us to respond accordingly:

“At the base of the Intelligence Seesaw is CQ, cultural intelligence, because that becomes fundamental. AQ, adaptability, is what changes the balance in real time.

“You can have IQ, EQ and SQ, but what moves the seesaw is your ability to adapt, to understand what’s going on and recognise which intelligence you are over- or under-indexing in that moment. IQ and EQ describe capability, but AQ determines whether that capability remains useful when the context changes.”

It’s not enough to know what to do and persist until we see results. We also need to recognise when the context has changed and adapt how we apply that knowledge.

Behaviour Only Becomes Sustainable When It Becomes Part of Who We Are

Sustainable change and long-term growth rely on one more step. The ideas we implement need to feel as though they belong to us.

The Growth Code co-author Lesley Everett shares that, “Until we make it part of us, nothing truly sticks forever. New behaviour becomes sustainable when repeated actions become personal beliefs.”

Our resistance to new ideas comes from an identity shaped by years of experience and reinforced beliefs. While that identity can obstruct change, it can also be what eventually makes change durable.

We need to evolve our identity as we learn and apply new ideas, moving from viewing those ideas as This isn’t me to This is how I work.

The Identity Evolution™
Source: (©) The Growth Code™ Used with permission

Everett and Nicklin stress the importance of coaching and culture in ensuring we make this identity transition. Leave people to navigate that transition alone, and old patterns can easily reassert themselves. But create space for conversation and exploration, in one-to-one and group environments, and meaningful change becomes more likely.

Individual change can then become collective. As behaviours are shared and reinforced, they begin to shape culture. As Nicklin observes, “Culture is what people observe. It’s what gets repeated. It’s what gets rewarded. It’s what gets tolerated.”

Organisations Don’t Change; People Do

Organisations might have the strategy, the people, and the desire to succeed. But none of those act by themselves. People throughout the business need to understand, apply, persist, adapt and internalise the knowledge that fuels growth.

And what makes this sustainable is what happens between people.

  • The manager who asks what someone has learned
  • The colleague who challenges or gives timely feedback
  • The coach who helps someone recognise and break down patterns of behaviour
  • The leader who gives permission to experiment and adapt
  • The team that recognises and reinforces positive new behaviour.

Organisations don’t change because someone in the team has learned something new. They change when we create an environment where those ideas take root, become new behaviours, and, eventually, become part of how we see ourselves and how we work together.

item.title: Why Uncertainty Can Feel Worse Than Bad News
item.description:
Anxiety

Why Uncertainty Can Feel Worse Than Bad News

What personality science says about why not knowing is so hard to sit with.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • People with higher emotional sensitivity often find uncertainty more distressing than confirmed bad outcomes.
  • Uncertainty intolerance is rooted in personality, and research shows this trait can shift.
  • Small, deliberate exposures to uncertainty build tolerance over time better than reassurance does.

A client of mine once described the week she spent waiting for a biopsy result as the worst of her life. She couldn't sleep, she couldn't concentrate, and she kept checking her phone for a call that didn't seem to be coming. When her doctor finally reached out with bad news, she said she was surprised to find that she felt relieved.

She didn't want bad news, of course. But it felt better to have an answer, rather than wait in limbo.

Why the Unknown Is Harder Than Bad News

Researchers who study intolerance of uncertainty have found that people differ substantially in how well they can function when an outcome isn't yet decided. Not knowing can trigger the same kind of anxiety response as a confirmed threat, and in some cases, a stronger one.

In one study, participants who were told they had a 50 percent chance of receiving a mild electric shock showed greater physiological stress than those who were told they'd definitely receive one. It seems that the uncertainty, not the threat itself, was harder to manage.

This makes sense. Your nervous system can adapt to a confirmed loss or difficulty because you can launch into problem-solving. When something is unresolved, the mind keeps running through possible scenarios but can't actually do anything about it.

What Personality Has to Do With It

If uncertainty throws you for a loop, your level of emotional sensitivity is likely a factor. Emotional sensitivity is the personality trait researchers refer to as neuroticism. It describes how easily and intensely you experience negative emotions.

People higher on this trait tend to notice potential problems more readily, respond to them more strongly, and take longer to return to baseline once activated. Uncertainty is the kind of trigger that keeps an activated nervous system running. There's no resolution to dampen the response, so your arousal stays high.

Although many people think personality is set in stone, ample research tells us that traits can change.

How to Build a Higher Tolerance

It's common for people who are troubled by uncertainty to seek reassurance. Unfortunately, getting reassurance that everything will work out OK is a temporary fix. Because we still don't know the outcome for sure, doubts creep back in.

What actually builds tolerance is practice with genuine not-knowing. The approach is to deliberately seek out small doses of uncertainty and sit with the uncomfortable feeling without trying to fix or solve anything. That could look like waiting an extra hour before checking your email for an important reply or making a low-stakes decision before you feel completely certain and observing what happens.

These small experiments teach you that you can, in fact, function with something unresolved hanging over your head. With this new evidence, over time, uncertainty stops registering as a threat signal you feel you must act on.

Of course, sometimes gathering more information before acting is the sensible move. The issue is when the discomfort of not knowing is what's driving your behavior, pushing you toward premature conclusions, repetitive checking, or reassurance-seeking that doesn't actually help.

item.title: The Similarities Between Therapy and Dating
item.description:
Therapy

The Similarities Between Therapy and Dating

The significance of the first meeting in finding the right match.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • First therapy sessions share many similarities with first dates.
  • We rely on our felt sense to tell us if we're likely to be a good match.
  • The relationship is key, and all the evidence supports the fact that this is where the healing happens.

I once arranged to meet a woman I didn’t know in an unfamiliar part of town. A mutual acquaintance set us up, as they thought we’d be a good match. I remember the trepidation as I decided what to wear for our first meeting and the nervous anticipation as I rang her doorbell. During the hour we spent together, I gradually relaxed. The conversation flowed easily, and she seemed interested in getting to know me, which helped calm my nerves and made me feel at ease. She was older than me and attractive: witty, nice hair, dressed in a similar style to my own. I could tell she’d made an effort, which pleased me, because I’d made an effort, too. We were a good match, and our relationship thrived long term.

Similarities Between Choosing a Therapist and Choosing a Partner

Choosing a therapist can feel like choosing a partner, and first sessions share many similarities with first dates. They’re risky and anxiety-provoking. We worry whether we’ll have enough to talk about, whether they’ll be kind and respectful, whether we’ll share the same relationship goals, and, ultimately, whether they’ll like us the same amount as we like them.

A potential therapist/date might be suggested by a mutual acquaintance, as mine was, or self-selected from an internet profile. For me, the relationship is key, and all the evidence supports the fact that this is where the healing happens.

I remember a first session with an outwardly confident 18-year-old full of swagger. He announced his arrival by hammering so loudly on the door I thought he might punch a hole through it. Once inside, he relaxed onto the couch without waiting to be invited and started talking immediately about family, friends, sexual encounters, and scrapes with authority. The hour flashed by. I’d found him charming and looked forward to seeing him again. He never returned, and he ignored all my calls. He’d enchanted me with his stories but wasn’t ready to commit. Our first session was the therapeutic equivalent of a one-night stand.

Another client bombarded me with emails before our first appointment because she wanted to “get a few things straight.” Her questions left me exhausted and anxious about our first session. She was a compact, buttoned-up young woman who didn’t take a breath as she recounted countless stories of being let down by “people like you.” She had low expectations that I’d be any different, but there was something about her I was drawn to, and I remember thinking how much I wanted to prove her wrong and offer her a more fulfilling relationship. And, against the odds, I did. Ours was an intense therapeutic relationship, full of passion and transferential hate, but we survived it and thrived.

Transference and Gut Instinct

First sessions, like first dates, contain a wealth of information about whether we’re a good match and how the relationship is likely to pan out. This is contained in the feeling response that therapists think of as transference and clients and daters think of as gut instinct. To allow this felt sense time to emerge, we need to be together and talk together and experience each other together. There’s an increased pressure to skip the “first date” stage of therapy and replace it with a “quick chat” consisting of a short, sharp Q and A that provides little room for emotional affect. For me, nothing meaningful can emerge during a “speed date,” and if that’s your preference, chances are we’re not a good match. I much prefer the opportunity to sit together, talk together, and experience each other together over a rich, luxurious, therapeutic hour.

It’s always a joy to meet someone you feel a connection with, who you’d like to see again, and who feels the same way, too. Herein lies the beginning of another beautiful relationship.

*Clinical vignettes are fictional and unrecognisable

item.title: How to Document Coercive Control for Court
item.description:
Domestic Violence

How to Document Coercive Control for Court

Calling abuse a “relationship conflict” lets the abuser off the hook.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • “Relationship conflict” can hide who is threatening, intimidating, or controlling whom.
  • Record the perpetrator’s actions, not just the atmosphere or problems in the relationship.
  • Good case notes make the pattern of coercion, its impact, and the person responsible easy to see.

"I'm going to kill you!"

A man screamed it inside a flat in Greater Manchester, loud enough that the words punched through the wall to the home next door. It was just after 4 p.m. on March 13, 2023, and the neighbour sat listening as the man kept shouting and hurling objects across the room. Then came a run of heavy thuds, sounds the neighbour would later tell police, like a body falling or being thrown down the stairs. A woman cried out in pain. Then the flat went silent.

The neighbour dialed 999.

Police reached the door within minutes. The man was already gone, and he had locked the door behind him as he left. When no one answered, officers forced their way in.

Inside, they found 33-year-old Danielle Haggerty near the top of the stairs, a ligature around her neck. She was unconscious and not breathing. Officers began CPR; paramedics restarted her heart, but the loss of oxygen had already caused irreversible brain damage. Three days later, her family made the decision to withdraw life support. Danielle was an organ donor. Her death saved the lives of three other people.

Later, investigators documented fresh bite marks on the man's forearms, indicating that a violent struggle had taken place inside the flat. The inquest concluded that she had died following an act of self-harm, at a time of distress, in the immediate aftermath of what it called a "violent argument," in a relationship it described as "volatile and abusive."

Yet a relationship cannot shout that it is going to kill someone. It cannot throw objects, or lock a door from the outside and walk away. Those were things a man did. The inquest's language dissolves all of that into a quarrel between two people. It makes the man who did it disappear. No one was prosecuted. The Crown Prosecution Service reviewed the case, declined to bring charges, and an independent review upheld that decision as correct. So on paper, this is a closed case: suicide, a tragedy with no perpetrator.

The Impact of Language in Describing Abuse

Consider two sentences:

“They had a volatile relationship.”

“He repeatedly threatened her, and she was afraid of what he would do.”

Reading the first sentence, you might be thinking, ''OK, there are two people who don't get along; perhaps they are not a good match." After you read the second sentence, you might actually start worrying about your client.

I explored this issue with family law barrister Joanna Toch, founder of Family Law Cafe, in a recent podcast conversation. For family lawyers and prosecutors, it can be helpful to look closely at how the story is being told. Is it clear who threatened, intimidated, or controlled whom, or have those actions become folded into a broader picture of “relationship conflict”? Keeping the perpetrator visible can make it easier to distinguish ordinary disagreement from coercion, and to avoid blurring the difference between experiencing abuse and causing it.

Who made the threats? Who controlled access to money? Who prevented the other person from leaving? Whose movements were restricted? Who was afraid, and what had the other person done to produce that fear? Without those details, recognising abuse does not necessarily mean recognising responsibility.

Words such as “volatile,” “toxic,” and “dysfunctional” can make this problem more pronounced. “Volatile” suggests unpredictability; “toxic” suggests that something about the combination of two people is harmful. Neither tells us whether one person was systematically threatening, punishing, or restricting the other.

The same problem appears in the word “argument.” Suppose a woman discovers that her partner has been monitoring her messages. She confronts him. He threatens her, and she shouts back. “The couple argued about her phone” records the topic and presents the interaction as shared. It leaves out the monitoring and the threat. A reader could come away thinking that the problem was poor communication about privacy. A more precise account would record the sequence: He monitored her messages; she challenged him; he threatened her; she shouted in response. There may be further facts to establish, but the actions are visible.

Clarity in Reporting and Recognising Abuse

If a record says “communication difficulties,” improving communication may appear to be the obvious task. If it describes repeated threats made when someone refuses a demand, the questions change. What happens when that person says no? Can they disagree safely? How is the threatening behaviour being addressed?

Similarly, “she keeps returning to an abusive relationship” makes her return the central action. The person abusing her recedes into the background. A fuller account would ask what happens around those returns. Does the perpetrator make promises, apply pressure, threaten consequences, exploit practical dependencies, or appeal to an existing emotional attachment? What options are available to her, and what does she believe will happen if she refuses contact? Her decisions remain part of the account. So do the actions of the person trying to influence them.

People can love someone who harms them. That attachment does not make the harm a joint undertaking. Nor does remaining emotionally invested explain away the other person’s decision to exploit that investment.

A short phrase may become the summary through which subsequent readers understand an entire history. If “relationship problems” is the summary, a later reader may never see the acts that made the situation dangerous. This is a practical concern for anyone writing case notes, assessments, referrals, or reports. Another professional should be able to identify the reported conduct without having to reconstruct it from vague descriptions.

Haggerty’s case requires that same care. We cannot infer that the wording of an inquest caused a decision not to prosecute. That would require evidence about the decision itself. But what we can examine is how a description distributes attention. Does it preserve the reported actions of particular people or compress them into the atmosphere of a relationship?

Even where someone dies by suicide, the actions of another person may remain legally relevant. In England and Wales, prosecution guidance explicitly recognises that murder or manslaughter may be considered where suicide follows another person’s unlawful conduct, including domestic abuse. Whether the evidence supports a charge is a separate question (Crown Prosecution Service guidance).

The wider lesson applies well beyond deaths and criminal proceedings. Friends, therapists, journalists, and professionals all make choices about how to describe abuse. Those choices can help keep the person responsible in view. We can say that someone experienced abuse from a partner. We can ask who did what, what pattern those actions formed, and how they affected the other person’s freedom and safety. The responsibility for abusive conduct belongs to the person who carries it out. Our language should make that responsibility easier to see.

item.title: Are You Running From or Running Toward?
item.description:
Decision-Making

Are You Running From or Running Toward?

Life offers us situations to avoid or embrace. How to tell the difference.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • There is a difference between running away and running toward something. Each has pros and cons.
  • Running away can be a sign of assertiveness or avoidance. Running toward can indicate passion or impulse.
  • Seeking closure after leaving helps prevent regret.
Source: theotherkev/Pixabay

Our lives can often feel like we’re on a track—always running—through our workday, running kids to football practice or ballet lessons, running just to get things done. But sometimes our running isn’t about the everyday; it's about something bigger, more serious—our job, a relationship—where it’s about major decisions and ultimately whether we are running from something or toward something.

They’re different, and each steers us toward a different path. Here are the pros and cons of each.

Running from

Pros: Running from something implies escape, and often that is exactly the purpose: to escape a toxic work environment or an emotionally or physically abusive relationship. Time to get out. Run away, run away. And if this decision and behavior are new to you—you’ve simply tolerated or accommodated in the past—this is also a testament to your growth and assertiveness.

Cons: Running away is not only about escape but, for some, often about avoidance. You quit your job or your relationship rather than taking the time and effort to work through the underlying problems. You never learn these important life lessons, and unsolved problems can pile up, becoming emotional roadblocks that, over time, make your world smaller and smaller as you try to work around them.

You also may be vulnerable to rebound jobs or relationships. If you jump into a new job or relationship too quickly, your view of the new can be colored by your view of the old. You understandably think in black-and-white terms—the three things you most disliked about the past job or partner. But as you emotionally recover, the initial glow fades; you notice problems you didn’t see at first. These are normal and new challenges to address, but if your style is to cut and run, you may, after a few months, repeat the pattern.

Finally, because running away can be about avoiding, you may never learn to stay still, face what is happening, and deal with it. This is not about the particular job or relationship but about how you handle anxiety and problems, and whether you can be proactive in solving them. This is about life skills that carry over into your life's challenges.

Running toward

Pros: A challenging new job and that new relationship feel exciting. Running toward is about embracing new possibilities, new passions, and new goals, seeing a challenge and accepting it—approaching rather than avoiding your anxiety.

Cons: The flip side of the coin remains—you’re avoiding problems by rushing forward instead of tackling them. Rather than carefully considering decisions, you run with whatever comes to mind first, whether it's the new shiny object, the dopamine hit, or what you feel like doing. Sometimes this works, and sometimes you regret it. Just as the running-away folks need to learn to face rather than avoid problems, your challenge is to slow down and make more rational, rather than impulsive, decisions.

So, what is the bridge between running from and running toward? Here are some suggestions.

Resist thinking in terms of either/or

Like many problems, it’s not about one extreme or the other, but something in the middle.

The middle is about problem-solving. Regardless of the situation, unless it is completely untenable, slow down and focus on the problems that need fixing: What are the one or two things—not 30—that would make the job or relationship better and help you feel the climate is improving?

Next, map out your ideal solution. You probably won’t get it, but knowing what you ultimately want gives you a strong starting point rather than a watered-down one.

If you decide to leave, get closure

The cut-and-run can come back to haunt you with regret or contaminate your future relationships; closure is important. Take action—say goodbye to colleagues, have that job exit interview or relationship-deconstruction conversation with your ex. Don’t leave things emotionally hanging.

Learn the lessons

Life isn’t about simply repeating patterns, but learning lessons. If you leave a job because it isn’t working, what did you learn about what to do next time? It may be about speaking up sooner, or asking tougher questions in the interview.

If you leave a relationship, avoid oversimplifying the moral of the story—he was angry, she was always critical. Drill down to uncover the micro-patterns in which you contributed to what unfolded. These more detailed lessons are what you want to carry forward so you don’t just repeat history.

Stepping back

So, when you look back on your past, have you tended to run away or run toward? Are there lessons your life is trying to teach you?

item.title: Meditation May Not Be for Everybody—and That’s OK
item.description:
Meditation

Meditation May Not Be for Everybody—and That’s OK

The emerging science of when meditation helps—and when it doesn’t.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Mindfulness may alter brain networks involved in attention, emotion, and self-referential thought.
  • Meditation can have adverse effects, including anxiety, and insomnia.
  • We need dose- and context-sensitive research on both the benefits and risks of meditation.

I will be the first to admit that I am an anxious type. I worry about little things and replay the events of the day in my mind.

I would like to be calmer and more collected, but that is simply not who I naturally am.

Meditation has helped bring some serenity into my life.

A few years ago, we stayed at a Shingon Buddhist temple on Kōyasan, where visitors were invited to practice Ajikan, a traditional form of Shingon meditation. We sat for about 45 minutes before breakfast and dinner, focusing on our breathing and on the Sanskrit letter A, traditionally visualized within a moon disc. I confess that I found it easier to substitute the image of a tree.

My tree for my meditation.
Source: Michiko Bruno

Still, I found the practice calming and rewarding.

Since then, I have tried to continue meditating with an app. But there always seems to be something more pressing, and I can’t say I have been a good student.

When I do manage to meditate, however, I am able to detach myself from my thoughts. Negative emotions; frustration, anger, and anxiety tend to recede. They are still there, but they matter less.

Neuroscience has begun to offer possible explanations for some of these effects. Studies suggest that mindfulness can alter activity and connectivity within and between brain networks involved in self-referential thought, emotional processing, and attentional control, including the default mode network, salience, and frontoparietal control networks.

I have also recommended meditation and breathing exercises to patients who seem anxious or stuck. And when we recommend a non-pharmacological intervention like meditation, we often add reassuringly: it’s safe. There is no harm in trying.

Can meditation have negative effects?

So when I recently read The Atlantic article, “When Meditation Has a Dark Side,” I was intrigued.

The article features research done by psychologist and meditation researcher Willoughby Britton. Britton was herself a meditation practitioner and originally entered the field studying meditation's benefits. Over time, she started to experience adverse effects with meditation, in her case, a sense of dissociation. She found others who experienced negative effects but also found that negative effects of meditation were rarely discussed openly in mindfulness research. In a 2017 study, she and her colleagues catalogued negative experiences associated with meditation, including anxiety, panic, insomnia, perceptual disturbances, derealization/depersonalization, altered sense of self, traumatic memories, mania-like states, and occasionally, psychosis.

The caveat here is that an experience that one person considers disturbing can be viewed as desirable by another, particularly when it involves changes in the sense of self. Defining an “adverse event” in meditation could therefore be surprisingly difficult. It is not like developing a rash or diarrhea from taking a pill. Yet, the study brought attention to something that has received relatively little scrutiny: Some meditators experience effects that are distressing rather than beneficial.

A subsequent systematic review evaluated 83 studies involving 6,703 participants and calculated a pooled prevalence of meditation-associated adverse events of about 8.3%. However, the estimates varied enormously across studies (I² approximately 95%), making the pooled figure difficult to interpret as a single estimate of risk.

How should we interpret these findings?

In some ways, the existence of adverse effects makes intuitive sense.

If meditation changes how we process attention, emotion, and our sense of self, why would we expect those changes to be beneficial in every person, at every dose, under every circumstance? An intervention capable of meaningfully altering the mind could, at least theoretically, also result in other changes. If meditation and mindfulness are truly beneficial overall, having zero adverse effects seems almost too good to be true.

I am therefore glad researchers are starting to ask these questions.

One of the early problems in meditation research may have been that the field rapidly grew in part through researchers who were themselves interested in or practitioners of meditation. That expertise can be valuable, but enthusiasm for an intervention can also introduce bias. Britton herself mentions this tension.

There are also other methodological considerations. For example, I have trouble imagining myself signing up for a multi-day silent meditation retreat. The people who do so may not be representative of the general population. Could some have pre-existing psychological vulnerabilities that both draw them toward intensive meditation and make adverse experiences more likely? That possibility creates a classic problem of selection bias.

Adverse events were reported in people with no previous mental health history, as well as people engaged in ordinary practice, so neither preexisting disease or intensity of the practice can explain everything. But intensive meditation retreat settings appear to deserve particular attention.

Meditation is not one thing

Perhaps the larger problem is that we talk about “meditation” as though it was a single intervention.

Ten minutes (if that) of self-guided breathing in my living room and multi-day silent meditation retreat are two completely different experiences. Calling both “meditation” is like putting walking the dog and running an ultramarathon into the same category of exercise.

If we want to understand meditation scientifically, we need to define it much more precisely. We need to study not only whether meditation “works” but how its effects vary according to the type of meditation, intensity, duration, sleep, prior experiences, mental health history, and perhaps even the reason someone chose to meditate in the first place.

What kind of meditation, at what dose, to produce which effects, in whom?

As of now, ordinary, moderate meditation has reasonable evidence of modest benefit and appears relatively low risk for most people. Adverse effect nevertheless exists and historically has been undermeasured.

Intensive practice deserves particular attention. Rare severe outcomes such as mania and psychosis have been documented but their incidence and causal risk factors remain poorly understood.

Overall, it makes meditation an intervention worthy of being studied with the same curiosity and skepticism we should bring to anything capable of changing the brain.

Meditation and mindfulness have become so widely embraced that they can sometimes feel less like options and more like things we should be doing. But perhaps we need to be careful not to moralize the practice. Meditation is not a virtue, and not enjoying it is not a failure.

Until we know more, meditation may be something worth trying, but it is probably best to follow the Dalai Lama’s advice on meditation: “It is helpful not to practice too long in the beginning; do not over-extend yourself."

And if your mind responds differently, or you simply don’t like it, that is OK—you don’t have to keep pushing yourself.

item.title: Homework vs. Sleep
item.description:
Sleep

Homework vs. Sleep

When to pull the plug on late-night studying.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • When homework spirals into mental overload, nothing more is going to get done.
  • Sacrificing rest sabotages the very brain functions needed to learn and stay regulated.
  • Regardless of why the work is delayed, define the endpoint in advance.

It’s midnight when my cellphone rings. On the line is my 16-year-old patient, overwhelmed by a sudden wave of panic. Her heart is racing, she’s in a cold sweat, and her thoughts feel like a cyclone. Through shallow breath and wobbling sobs, she reveals the trigger: a 10-page paper due tomorrow that she only started yesterday. Paralyzed by the fear of failing, she is stuck.

I sit up, turn on my bedside light, and shake the sleep from my brain. We start with the most urgent need: slowing down her breathing to calm her nervous system. Counting breaths is all her brain can handle right now, so that’s where we begin. Once her breathing settles, I offer a solution that shocks her: put away the homework and go to bed.

She pushes back, terrified of the consequences. But I give her the same reasoning I give every patient in this situation: No productive work is getting done tonight. Your brain is exhausted. Sleep now, and problem-solve in the morning. While discussions with her parents and teacher will still need to happen, facing tomorrow on zero sleep will only guarantee a worse outcome.

Over the years, as this young person grew into an adult, we revisited that midnight conversation repeatedly—through college and into her professional life—reinforcing the vital principle of prioritizing sleep over deadlines to remain healthy and resilient.

Source: Lightfield Studios/Shutterstock

The Online Debate: Blame vs. Solutions

Whenever I share this perspective online, many parents, educators, and clinicians applaud the message. Yet, predictably, internet discussions bring strong pushback. The arguments usually center on assignations of blame:

  • Parents: They must be giving their kids too much or too little structure.
  • Students: They aren’t doing their work at school and/or their wasting time at home—poor time management.
  • Screens: Attributing late-night stress entirely to phones and video games.
  • Teachers: Blaming teachers for too much homework or blaming me for suggesting that teachers give too much homework.
  • Denial of the problem: Stating that no child is staying up too late to do homework—it’s never homework.

While these points reflect important and complex challenges for today’s families, they miss the fundamental clinical point. Regardless of why the work remains unfinished—whether it’s due to overscheduling, too much screen time, refusing to do the work, or excessive workload—there comes a point in the evening when the work must stop.

The Dangerous Spiral of Sleep Deprivation

Putting off sleep to complete homework creates a dangerous physiological and psychological spiral. Chronic sleep deprivation directly impairs:

  • Physical health and immune function.
  • Focus, memory, and executive function.
  • Mood regulation and impulse control.
  • Critical problem-solving capabilities.
  • Safety during high-risk activities like driving.

A recurring habit of sacrificing sleep for homework is profoundly counterproductive. A brain starved of rest cannot process, learn, or retain new information effectively.

Two Principles for Healthy Evening Boundaries

To protect sleep and lower evening anxiety, keep two clinical principles in mind:

1. Bedtime Is About Rest, Not Forced Sleep

You cannot force a child or teenager to fall asleep. Attempting to do so only increases frustration. Instead, focus on creating environments and routines that quiet the body and mind. Shutting down demands and transitioning into rest opens the door for natural sleep.

2. Technology Belongs Outside the Bedroom

Screens interfere with the brain’s ability to wind down. Establishing a family-wide tech policy—where all phones and computers are stored outside bedrooms overnight—provides crucial structural support. Because teenagers often view their phones as a primary social lifeline, discuss these boundaries with empathy and problem-solve their distress together rather than imposing harsh penalties.

Moving From Punishment to Curiosity

If a child consistently struggles to finish homework before a reasonable shutdown time, punishment will not solve the issue. Persistent struggles require curiosity and compassion. The underlying cause might be:

  • An overwhelming workload mismatch.
  • An unidentified learning challenge.
  • Executive function difficulties associated with ADHD.
  • Underlying anxiety or depression.
  • Illness or pain.
  • Many other possibilities beyond “being difficult.”

If late-night homework battles are a routine occurrence in your household, start with collaborative conversations with your child and be curious about their concern—involve them in this process. Reach out to the teacher for their perspective, consider workload adjustments or learning concerns, and consult your pediatrician to explore other potential underlying causes.

Final Thoughts

Nightly arguments over homework versus sleep do not mean your child is lazy or difficult. Prioritizing rest over incomplete tasks is the necessary first step toward meaningful change—because a mind that is too exhausted to function cannot learn new ways to thrive.
